---
title: "02. Gauss–Seidel: a sequential in-place sweep"
description: "Each update reads values updated a moment earlier in the same sweep. Natural as a loop, awkward as an array program."
jupyter: python3
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
import weanj
import pandas as pd
EXAMPLE = "02-gauss-seidel"
res = weanj.load_results(EXAMPLE)
timed = res[res.grad_s.notna()]
def t(impl, device, variant, n, col="grad_s"):
    row = timed[(timed.impl == impl) & (timed.device == device) & (timed.variant == variant) & (timed.n == n)]
    return float(row[col].iloc[0]) if len(row) else float("nan")
def ms(v):
    if v != v:
        return "not run (over time budget)"
    return f"{v:.1f} s" if v >= 1 else f"{1e3 * v:.1f} ms" if v >= 1e-3 else f"{1e6 * v:.0f} µs"
def ratio(a, b):
    return f"{a / b:.0f}×" if a / b >= 10 else f"{a / b:.1f}×"
```

## The problem

Solve $-\Delta u = \theta$ on the unit square ($n \times n$ interior points, $u = 0$ on the
boundary) with $K$ Gauss–Seidel sweeps from $u = 0$, and differentiate
$$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \lVert u_K(\theta) - u_{\text{obs}} \rVert^2$$
with respect to the source $\theta$. Each update is
$$u_{ij} \leftarrow \tfrac14\left(h^2\theta_{ij} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i+1,j} + u_{i,j-1} + u_{i,j+1}\right),$$
**in place**: $u_{i-1,j}$ and $u_{i,j-1}$ are values already updated earlier in the
same sweep. That is what makes Gauss–Seidel converge about twice as fast as Jacobi,
and it is what makes it a sequential loop.

The same pattern appears in SOR, incomplete factorisations, the Thomas algorithm,
upwind sweeps and line relaxation.

Two variants:

- **Lexicographic**, the textbook sweep: a triple loop.
- **Red-black**, which colours the grid like a chessboard so that each colour can be
  updated in parallel. It is a *different iteration*, with a different result, and it is
  the formulation a GPU or JAX user writes. Gradients are compared within each variant.

## Same gradient

$n = 32$, $K = 20$, Float64. Each gradient is also checked against finite differences.

```{python}
#| echo: false
for variant, impls in (("lexicographic", ("enzyme-lex", "reactant-lex", "jax-lex")),
                       ("red-black", ("enzyme-rb", "reactant-rb", "jax-rb"))):
    cmp = weanj.compare_gradients(EXAMPLE, impls=impls)
    display(cmp.style.hide(axis="index").set_caption(variant)
            .format({cmp.columns[1]: "{:.6e}", cmp.columns[2]: "{:.1e}"}))
```

## Timings

$K = 100$ sweeps, Float64, median of 3–10 runs after warm-up. A sweep stops once a
single gradient takes more than 5 s.

```{python}
#| echo: false
weanj.scaling_plot(EXAMPLE, "grad_s", "Gradient time vs grid points (K = 100)",
                   query="K == 100 and grad_s == grad_s", x_label="grid points n²")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
weanj.scaling_plot(EXAMPLE, "forward_s", "Forward time vs grid points (K = 100)",
                   query="K == 100 and forward_s == forward_s", x_label="grid points n²")
```

## What this shows

**The sequential sweep on the CPU.** At $n = 512$ the lexicographic gradient takes
`{python} ms(t("enzyme", "cpu", "lexicographic", 512))` with Enzyme and
`{python} ms(t("jax", "cpu", "lexicographic", 512))` with JAX, although their forward
passes are close (`{python} ms(t("enzyme", "cpu", "lexicographic", 512, "forward_s"))` and
`{python} ms(t("jax", "cpu", "lexicographic", 512, "forward_s"))`). Enzyme's gradient costs
`{python} ratio(t("enzyme", "cpu", "lexicographic", 512), t("enzyme", "cpu", "lexicographic", 512, "forward_s"))`
its forward pass; JAX's costs
`{python} ratio(t("jax", "cpu", "lexicographic", 512), t("jax", "cpu", "lexicographic", 512, "forward_s"))`.
JAX expresses the sweep as nested `lax.scan`s, and the transposed scan of a scan does
much more work per step than the scalar loop it came from.

**The sequential sweep on the GPU.** At $n = 64$ the lexicographic gradient takes
`{python} ms(t("jax", "gpu", "lexicographic", 64))` with JAX and
`{python} ms(t("reactant", "gpu", "lexicographic", 64))` with Reactant, against
`{python} ms(t("enzyme", "cpu", "lexicographic", 64))` for Enzyme on one CPU core. Every
scalar update becomes a step of an XLA loop, which on the GPU means a device round trip
per grid point. Reactant traces the same Julia triple loop as Enzyme, so the language is
not the issue: the loop is slow once it goes through XLA.

**Memory does not grow with K, for either tool.** We expected reverse mode through
$K$ in-place sweeps to store $K$ copies of $u$. It doesn't, because each update is
*linear*: its derivative is the constant $\tfrac14$, so the backward pass needs no
stored values. Both Enzyme's activity analysis and JAX's linearisation see this.

```{python}
#| echo: false
mem = res[(res.variant == "lexicographic") & (res.n == 256) & (res.device == "cpu")]
mem = mem.assign(MiB=(mem.peak_mem_bytes / 2**20).round(2))
mem.pivot_table(index="K", columns="impl", values="MiB").style.format("{:.2f}").set_caption(
    "Gradient memory [MiB], lexicographic, n = 256 (Enzyme: bytes allocated by the call; JAX: XLA temp buffers)")
```

A nonlinear sweep, such as nonlinear Gauss–Seidel with a local Newton step, would need
stored values in both tools and make memory a real issue. That is not tested here.

## Where JAX wins / what we did not do

::: {.callout-note}
**Red-black on the GPU is where the XLA tools shine.** At $n = 1024$ the red-black
gradient takes `{python} ms(t("reactant", "gpu", "red-black", 1024))` with Reactant,
`{python} ms(t("jax", "gpu", "red-black", 1024))` with JAX and
`{python} ms(t("enzyme", "gpu", "red-black", 1024))` with Enzyme through
KernelAbstractions; on small grids Enzyme is several times slower. Enzyme launches two
kernels per sweep, forward and reverse, while XLA compiles the whole loop into one
program. That launch overhead dominates on small
grids.
:::

- A JAX expert can rewrite the lexicographic sweep without a scalar loop. Along each
  column the update is a first-order linear recurrence, which
  `jax.lax.associative_scan` evaluates in parallel. That is a different algorithm, with
  different rounding and $O(\log n)$ depth, and you have to know the trick.
- No Enzyme multithreading and no fused multi-sweep GPU kernel.
